sn10.1:1.1: Compare Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.8: “When at birth this person takes on a body, he becomes united with bad things, and when at death he leaves it behind, he gets rid of those bad things” (Olivelle’s translation). This shares many terms with Indaka’s verse: use of _ayaṁ_ for the subject; _sarīra_ for the body; _sajjati_ for _saṁsṛjyate_. Furthermore, the “bad things” are explained in the commentary as the body and organs with which the soul becomes burdened at birth. This passage is part of the dialogue on the “light of a person” between Yājñavalkya and Janaka, which is alluded to many times in the Pali Suttas.
sn10.1:1.2: The _yakkha_ Indaka is named after the mountain he inhabits. The mountain itself might be identified with Mount Vediyaka, where Sakka/Indra appeared to the Buddha at Indra’s hill cave ([dn21:1.1.2]()). Indaka’s interest in human fertility stems from the role such _yakkhas_ played in both fertility and death of children, for which he would have been offered sacrifices.
sn10.1:2.1: While this exact wording (_rūpaṁ na jīvan_) doesn’t seem to be a direct quote of the Buddha, it is a similar to _taṁ jīvaṁ taṁ sarīraṁ_, which the Buddha did indeed deny. Taken by itself, of course, this does not deny that there *is* a soul, only that it is not physical. The use of _jīva_ for soul, rather than _attā_, is characteristic of the Jains, but is used by Vedists as well. It seems Indaka’s question is how an immortal soul can be bound to an organic body.
sn10.1:2.2: Indaka uses the Upaniṣadic style, indicating a subject with _ayaṁ_ (“this one”) which is assumed to be the immortal Self or Person. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.8 has _sa vā ayaṁ puruṣo_, referring back the previous sentence, “this person made of consciousness amid the organs, the light in the heart” (_ayaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu hṛdyantarjyotiḥ puruṣaḥ_).
sn10.1:2.3: Perhaps “organs” would be better for _yakapiṇḍa_ here.
sn10.1:2.4: Bodhi (*Connected Discourses*, note 559) proposes deriving _sajjati_ from _sṛj_, which he renders “begotten”. This is born out by the Upaniṣad’s _saṁsṛjyate_, which has the senses of being “created” and being “joined”.
sn10.1:3.1: “Zygote” is _kalala_, a newly fertilized ovum, described in the commentary as “no more than a drop of cream of ghee on a single fibre of lamb’s wool”.
sn10.1:3.2: “Blastocyst” is _abbuda_, otherwise used of a tumor or cancer. This fits the blastocyst, which is implanted in the uterine wall about a week after conception, a detail noted in the commentary. For other meanings, see notes on [sn1.77:1.4]() and [snp3.10:8.2]().
sn10.1:3.3: “Gastrula” renders _pesi_, literally “scrap of flesh”. The embryo, only a few millimeters long, is forming distinct layers and emerging from the uterine wall.
sn10.1:3.4: The “embryo with organs” (_ghana_, literally “lump”) sees the formation of internal organs starting around the fourth week. As the limbs have not yet appeared, the commentary says it looks like a chicken egg.
sn10.1:3.5: According to the commentary, this is around the fifth week, which once again correlates fairly well with medical facts.
